New on our Engineering blog: Creating in-house source control. 

In May, we merged around 2,500 code changes per day. In September, we merged more than 30,000 per day. As a result, we became bottlenecked by developer infrastructure built for human (rather than agent) scale.  

Here, we share how we built a new version control system—and fully migrated our monorepo from git—in five months: https://t.co/wzNkwHs7IN

items.content:
Gemini 4 Argon is now GA. Argon ranks equal to GPT-6 Astra on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60% of the Cost per Task with discounted prices until Nov 30

Key takeaways:
- Google is back to having a frontier model released to the public: This is Google's first proprietary model above the Flash class in over 7 months

- Pricing temporarily discounted to 50% until November 30: Gemini 4 Argon has a Cost per Task of $1.99 with discounted prices, a ~40% reduction compared to GPT-6 Astra (max) for a comparable level of Intelligence. It is currently priced at $2/$10 per 1M input/output tokens with a 95% discount for cache reads (up from 90% from previous Gemini models). Prices will increase to $4/$20 after November 30

- Large improvements in agentic performance: Gemini 4 Argon shows substantial improvements in agentic evaluations such as AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal Bench 4. This is an area in which Google's models have historically underperformed compared to leading peers

Lowest hallucination rate among leading models: On AA-Omniscience, Gemini 4 Argon has a 15% hallucination rate, the lowest of any model scoring 45+ on the Intelligence Index

items.title: I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over pr...
items.content:
I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over previous Gemini models and it is the first non-OpenAI/Anthropic model to pass the Fable/Mythos/Astra bar. It is also much more pleasant and more agentic then previous Gemini models, without the weird personality issues that you often found in Gemini 3 series models. In fact, a big advantage is that has a very different personality and sense of taste than Claude or Astra, making it a good addition to the AI world. 

On the usefulness side, in some areas it is at least at par with OpenAI and Anthropic (it is quite creative and a good writer), but in others it lags, including at complex multi-agent work. It has a tendency to be too certain about its conclusions and a little lazy, issues not helped by the Antigravity harness not being quite as good as the competition. Still, I expect to see rapid improvements in model abilities using Gemini 4 as a base.

Here is a fun example:  "create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and inuitive to people who just want to play, but are sophisticated and deep for people who know something about architecture. you should be able to play a lot with design and approach. there should be simulation modes and different ways to view or experience the city. make it stunning. i want to host this on netlify in the end"

items.title: Excited to share ReRoute, our new framework for scientific counterfactual prediction: informed by pa...
items.content:
Excited to share ReRoute, our new framework for scientific counterfactual prediction: informed by partial physics knowledge for much better generalization. 🌍

AI models can be remarkably accurate on familiar data, yet struggle with scientific ‘what-if’ questions

The key idea: Combine observational data with partial physical knowledge to predict unseen interventions—without requiring new controlled experiments.

Instead of retraining models on expensive new simulations, ReRoute uses known partial physical mechanisms to guide pretrained models through lightweight fine-tuning on existing data.

The results:
🌍 Up to 31.8% lower prediction error under severe CO₂ distribution shifts in climate emulators.
🔬 Up to 89.6% lower counterfactual error in controlled advection–diffusion experiments.
⚡ No new intervention data. No retraining from scratch. Just lightweight fine-tuning.

We also establish a causal identification result under explicit structural assumptions, with a machine-checked proof in Lean.

The bigger picture: Scientific AI doesn't always need more data or bigger models to generalize beyond what it has seen. Sometimes, knowing just a little about how the world works can make a big difference. @Dingling_Yao @kahaan_gandhi @FrancescoLocat8 @Caltech 

📄 Paper: https://t.co/dmvUwLdOJN
#AIforScience #ScientificML #ClimateAI #CausalInference #PhysicsAI

items.title: In 2024, Character AI said it was answering 20,000 messages a second, around a fifth of what Google ...
items.content:
In 2024, Character AI said it was answering 20,000 messages a second, around a fifth of what Google Search handled.

In September 2025, Disney’s lawyers ordered it to pull every Disney character off the app.

Last month, ex-CEO Karandeep Anand left to become Disney’s CTO, and some of his staff went with him.

On Monday, Character AI filed for bankruptcy.

Now, Disney is bidding $20M to license parts of Character AI’s tech, and those ex-employees will help keep the app running during the sale.

Other buyers can still outbid Disney before the auction wraps. If nobody steps in, the company says it will shut down.

items.title: we are thinking a lot about how to make deepagents more async native. specifically about making asyn...
items.content:
we are thinking a lot about how to make deepagents more async native. specifically about making async subagents work better/more prominent

one key question is how does a finished subagent "notify" the parent agent? some default behaviors we're considering for when the parent is still running:

1/ interrupt parent run, apply subagent update, continue (basically same as "steer")

2/ wait for parent run to finish, then batch subagent update with any other new messages (basically same as "queue")

another question is how to handle human in the loop? what if main agent is not running but paused and waiting explicit human response to an action?

a/ wait for human to respond, then batch the subagent update with that

b/ resume thread (which would cancel the human interrupt) with the subagent update (thread could then re-ask for the same human approval)

any other options we're missing?

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Character .ai filed for bankruptcy, going from a $2.7 billion Google deal to a ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Character .ai filed for bankruptcy, going from a $2.7 billion Google deal to a $20 million Disney sale.

• Disney is paying $20M for some assets and a perpetual license to its tech, and the platform shuts down if no buyer keeps it running
• Founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas left Google in 2021 after it refused to release Meena, the chatbot they built there
• In 2024, Google paid $2.7B to license its tech and rehire them. Shazeer helped turn Gemini around, then left for OpenAI in under 2 years
• It peaked at 20M monthly users, then faced lawsuits over teen safety, including a settled case over a 14-year-old's suicide
• It lost its top talent twice, to Google and then to Disney along with its CEO last month, banned under-18 users and cut open-ended chat
• The rest of AI has growing users and few legal headwinds, so this isn't a sign of a bust, but it previews what heavy regulation could do

@theojaffee: "So basically, like it's the worst possible scenario for a startup. They lost their top tech talent multiple times."

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: ByteDance just set up China's first standalone safety and alignment department at a frontier AI lab.

• Led by Yan Lin, Seed's new Model-Alignment & Preparedness department absorbs its Responsible AI team and part of its Chat team
• It'll focus on agent safety and CBRN risks through model specs, safety evals, alignment training and risk monitoring, much like US labs
• Until now, Chinese labs folded safety into general security and compliance teams
• The idea that Chinese labs ignore safety is a caricature. Market incentives push them toward alignment, and so does the fear of losing control
• China has more people doing third-party model evals than the US, and Seed plans to work more with outside evaluators
• Seed is even hiring in San Jose, LA and Seattle

@theojaffee: "I think people should not be so fatalistic about the potential for coordination between the US and China, you know, as we have done for many years in many areas."

items.content:
There are 4 specialized execution paths here:

• Classification
• Extraction
• Summarization
• Context Compression

The architecture behind classification and span extraction in their white paper is really cool:

They have a task-specific head that reads the input's internal representation and selects a label or source span. This avoids autoregressive token generation for the prediction itself.

As a result, classification returns labels from the supplied set. Extraction returns text from the input, along with source offsets and confidence scores.

The model can still choose the wrong label or passage, but restricting the answer space makes its outputs easier to validate.

items.title: Decision models offer significant speed and cost advantages over language models, but trail on knowl...
items.content: Decision models offer significant speed and cost advantages over language models, but trail on knowledge and reasoning. On classification and tool-calling tasks, leading decision models perform comparably to language models while being significantly faster and cheaper. However, language models outperform on knowledge and reasoning. Claude Haiku 5.5 (Low) scores 61 on the Decision Index, 3 points ahead of Jev 1.13, but takes 1.4 seconds per task vs. 0.13 seconds (11x slower) and costs $184 per 1M Tasks vs. $42 for Jev 1.13 (4.4x more expensive)

They're all pretty good! 
- Muse Spark and Gemini 4 Argon* are SOTA at their respective price points for table understanding among frontier models. 
- Wonder and Argon are also quite good at chart understanding, reading order, and formatting recognition

We're committed to open benchmarking of all available models even as we aim to build the best specialized models for document parsing and extraction.

After much testing and talking to actual users across all three proactive AI agents:

Muse - best one for your parents, heavy IG/FB users, people who like or need easy setups, people who don’t want to build anything, best use case idea generator by a mile (aka great if you don’t know what you want to use it for but you have to click the idea tab!), best for people who still say “wtf can AI do for me” 

Dots - best for OpenAI users, people who might need to build/code, people who deal with slack a lot, people who love voice features

Instinct - people who live in their iMessage/don’t want to open another app, people who don’t need crazy fancy visualizations, people who want internet watchdogs (like “next time AJ Jacobs writes an article, send it to me”), easiest setup (tied with Muse)

I am a very heavy Instinct user and light Muse/Dots user, largely because it's in iMessage.

Muse also made several basic mistakes when I was chatting with it and forgot things after awhile. Didn’t feel like a state of the art model, despite somewhat equal benchmarks to Astra on GDPval-AA, but that might change with today's new model news, so I'm excited to test.

And my honest take: still feels just very early across the space. We're going to see more. 

Note: answers subject to change, literally day by day.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, beats GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5....
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, beats GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 on most benchmarks.

• Google's demo has it build a photorealistic pagoda in Blender from 1 prompt, using blueprints, Nano Banana references and a multi-agent loop where a critic checks every render
• Its biggest lead is Harvey's legal agent benchmark: 19.6%, nearly 3x the next best. It trails on Terminal-bench, FrontierSWE and OSWorld
• It's rolling out in the Gemini app for AI Pro and Ultra, and in Antigravity for Ultra only
• It can write up to 1M tokens in a single response, up from 64K
• 18 months ago, o1, o3 and DeepSeek R1 couldn't use Blender at all
• Modeling Versailles or the Titanic's interior once needed a funded team. Now it just takes tokens

@theojaffee: "This might be by far the best 3D model I've ever seen from an AI."

items.title: Fish Audio's Drama 3 Preview is the new #1 open-weights Text to Speech model on the Artificial Analy...
items.content:
Fish Audio's Drama 3 Preview is the new #1 open-weights Text to Speech model on the Artificial Analysis Text to Speech leaderboard. The model also leads all models in our Pronunciation Robustness leaderboard, ahead of Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo

Drama 3 Preview is the new open weights Text to Speech model from @FishAudio, built for multi-character scenes and long-form content with voice cloning and natural-language control. Weights are available on Hugging Face under the Fish Audio Community License.

Key takeaways:

➤ Pronunciation Robustness: Drama 3 Preview scores 93.2%, ranking #1 ahead of Eleven v4 at 91.7% and Eleven v4 Turbo at 90.1%. It ranks #1 in Standalone Terms and Preserving Exact Sequences and #2 in Expanding Shorthand.

➤ Provider Voice: Drama 3 Preview has an Elo of 1,243 (+16/-16) across 1,857 appearances, ranking #10, a 101 point gain on the previous Fish Audio S2.1 Pro at 1,142.

➤ Controlled Voice: Drama 3 Preview ranks #14 with an Elo of 1,058 (+15/-15) across 1,804 appearances.

➤ Open weights: Drama 3 Preview is the #1 open weights model on all three of our Text to Speech leaderboards. On Pronunciation Robustness it leads the next open weights model, Mistral's Voxtral TTS at 78.1%, by 15 points, and in the Provider Voice Arena it is ahead of Breeze TTS 2 at 1,221. Drama 3 is a 35B parameter mixture-of-experts model (3B active) supporting 83 languages, available on Hugging Face.

➤ Pricing: Drama 3 Preview is available via the Fish Audio API at $15/1M characters, the same as S2.1 Pro, compared to Eleven v4 at $80/1M characters and Eleven v4 Turbo at $40/1M characters.

See more details and listen to samples below 🧵

Right now it still takes, let's say, 30 minutes to a few ho...
items.content:
This is also interesting to think about

Right now it still takes, let's say, 30 minutes to a few hours to build something usable with AI and then you still polish for days/weeks/months

If we assume this will keep getting faster, at some point an AI model will take a second or less to generate the whole thing

Imagine a future where you can create anything in less than second?

How will that change what we choose to create? Will humans even create, or will it all be AI agents coming up with ideas themselves?

The next constraints then become physical? If AI can generate for example hardware plans so fast, it will still take 30 minutes to 3d print that, so maybe the next speed and intelligence optimizations will then start happening in hardware, being able to generate an idea and producing a physical object in a minute or so

I have no idea but very interesting, it's kinda like those real-time video models we saw last month (like my Infinite Slop project), how will content change if you can generate so fast?

🤔

items.title: Factory's @TaylorTheSavage argues that Claude Code and Codex aren't necessarily the best tools for t...
items.content:
Factory's @TaylorTheSavage argues that Claude Code and Codex aren't necessarily the best tools for their own AI models, and third-party harnesses can actually outperform them:

"One thing that I deeply believed before I started at Factory was that the harnesses created by the model companies are going to be the best for their models. Claude Code is going to be the best for Anthropic models, obviously, and Codex is going to be the best for OpenAI models, obviously."

"Starting at Factory, I realized that is just not true at all. You can actually do a lot better than those harnesses, certainly on specific types of workloads, but also even in the general case. Different incentives than you have if you’re building a third-party harness."

"Keeping them separate also allows you to not get too overfit towards one model. You need to be able to delegate between the different models, not just models from one particular company."

"Like Shelby Cobra, you’ve got tuners of cars that can take a car that’s built by Ford and make it work better than it rolled off the factory line. You get things coming out from one OEM, and then you’ve got other people that tune it aftermarket. I think that’s absolutely true with harnesses and models."
@FactoryAI

"Keeping them separate also allows you to not get too overfit towards one model. You need to be able to delegate between the different models, not just models from one particular company."

"Like Shelby Cobra, you’ve got tuners of cars that can take a car that’s built by Ford and make it work better than it rolled off the factory line. You get things coming out from one OEM, and then you’ve got other people that tune it aftermarket. I think that’s absolutely true with harnesses and models."

@FactoryAI

"Being able to find that vulnerability and then actually patch it, this is one example of hopefully something that will scale."

items.title:
Searching data using semantic similarity alone is flawed. Graph-aware retrieval is the way to go.

T...
items.content:
Searching data using semantic similarity alone is flawed. Graph-aware retrieval is the way to go.

The basic implementation runs flat retrieval to select records that match a query. This ranks records by semantic similarity and returns the closest matches from the store.

This works well when you store the information you need in independent records, but it fails when you need to understand relationships between facts.

Graph-aware retrieval is a huge upgrade.

It has three components:

1. It stores facts as persistent memory records

2. It connects records with directed links labeled with their relationships. For example, "supersedes," "supports," or "contradicts"

3. It expands search results by going through the links and returning every connected record

Because of this, your query results will contain both matching facts and information about their relationships.

Imagine you have two stored conversations:

• "The meeting is on Monday."
• "The meeting has moved to Tuesday."

If you use a simple flat search to answer, "When is the meeting?", you'll get both records back because they match the question.

If you use graph-aware retrieval, you will get back a "superseeds" relationship showing that Tuesday replaces Monday.

Oracle AI Agent Memory 26.8 implements graph-aware search. You can read their technical walkthrough and check out the code here:

https://t.co/7gQIbQN1GT

Thanks to the @OracleDevs team for partnering with me on this post.

"The use cases that it’s gonna be particularly useful for are these deep, deep reasoning use cases. Think scientific research, open math problems. These are cases where the model does need to reason a lot in a single step to get you a really strong outcome."

"If you cap the model at 64K tokens, it isn’t able to do that full set of reasoning. By enabling the model to go longer, it does better on these more complex reasoning tasks."
@GoogleDeepMind

"The good thing the EA movement has been teaching us is that we need to take these AI safety risks seriously."

"Safety is not a static concept. It’s not a one-and-done thing. Real safety comes from ongoing experimentation and iterative trial and error, not through one-shot centralized controls and interventions. It’s very messy."

"People want simple playbooks. They want silver bullets, especially policymakers. Tell us the plan. It’s not always that easy."

"We see this debate reflected in how Dario Amodei talks about these issues versus Jensen at NVIDIA or Mark Zuckerberg. A real conflict of vision between the open source community and the closed source proprietary providers. This is the heart of the future of AI policy."

items.title: Cache hit rates and Cost per Task by provider are now live on Artificial Analysis: Cost per Task for...
items.content:
Cache hit rates and Cost per Task by provider are now live on Artificial Analysis: Cost per Task for GLM-5.3 (max) varies ~9x across providers, driven by a combination of cache hit rate and token pricing

Agentic workloads resend the full conversation history every turn, so most input tokens are cacheable, and cache pricing and cache hit rates drive most of the gap in Cost per Task. We already use measured cache hit rates to calculate Cost per Task, and are now publishing them for each model endpoint we track.

What's new:
➤ Cache hit rates are now visible for all first-party and third-party endpoints, measured by running multi-turn agentic coding tasks and reading cached tokens from each provider's usage response. Cache hit rate is the share of cacheable input tokens served from cache.
➤ Cost per Task is now available by provider for open weights models, calculated from each provider's input, output, cache hit and cache write prices, applied at its measured cache hit rate. To standardize across providers for a given model, we use the same input, output and cacheable token counts from the model's Intelligence Index run.

Key takeaways:
➤ Cost per Task on GLM-5.3 (max) spans ~9x across providers, from $0.92 on Makora to $8.68 on Nebius. Both serve nearly all cacheable input from cache (98% and 100%) and charge the same output price ($4.40 per 1M tokens), so the gap comes from input pricing: Makora charges $0.10 per 1M cached input tokens, while Nebius offers no cached input discount on its shared serverless endpoints and bills all input at the full $1.40.
➤ Cache hit rate ranges from 41% to 100% across 21 providers (25 endpoints). 15 endpoints are at 98% or above, and eight are at 100%: Modal, DeepInfra, Parasail, Together AI, DigitalOcean, Nebius, Novita and Z AI's first-party API. Multiverse Computing is lowest at 41%, followed by Bitdeer at 50%.

items.content:
Euronews replaced human narrators in their news clips with AI. Today, I felt like I was listening to a dead person speaking.

I think the backlash that we observe against AI among normal people all over the world isn't about what AI can do (normal people are mostly unaware), but about this uncanny valley that they now feel everywhere they go: from funny cat videos to their favorite news outlets to their coworkers' emails.

items.title: AIUC CEO @RuneKvist warns that autonomous AI agents could create a dangerous legal loophole where re...
items.content:
AIUC CEO @RuneKvist warns that autonomous AI agents could create a dangerous legal loophole where real-world damage occurs but nobody is held responsible:

"The frame we work in is, how do you build markets with teeth? The first level of that is liability, and the second level is insurance."

"A lot of the existing law will apply somewhat straightforwardly. There’s gonna be a bunch of new questions where there’s no human intent, say in the case of Hugging Face, and then it’s for courts to interpret what happens with liability."

"There’s a bill put forward this week that when an agent causes damage, someone should be held liable. It can’t be no one. Who that is might differ case by case. It’s extremely important that there’s no gap where no one is liable."

"Patching the current liability system is an extremely effective lever for creating the clarity that insurance markets thrive on."
@aiunderwriting

items.title: Modern AI increasingly relies on Large Reasoning Models that produce step-by-step intermediate think...
items.content:
Modern AI increasingly relies on Large Reasoning Models that produce step-by-step intermediate thinking traces before outputting a final response. While this test-time computation generally boosts performance, it has remained uncertain whether the final answer actually depends on these intermediate traces or if the thinking steps are merely cosmetic, post-hoc explanations.

This article evaluates this question by systematically investigating the functional and informational connection between intermediate reasoning traces and final answers in three distilled DeepSeek R1 models.

The authors use a three-stage experimental framework combining black-box empirical benchmarks, internal attention mechanism analysis, and mechanistic causal interventions.

They evaluate model responses on the MATH-500 mathematical benchmark and the multi-domain WildBench dataset, both with intermediate reasoning enabled and explicitly suppressed. They then map how answer tokens direct their attention toward reasoning tokens across network layers. Finally, the authors apply activation patching—a causal tracing technique where internal neural activations are swapped between contrasting prompt pairs—to measure whether targeted alterations to intermediate reasoning directly alter the generated final answer.

items.title: Organizations increasingly depend on AI to extract insights from structured knowledge bases across h...
items.content:
Organizations increasingly depend on AI to extract insights from structured knowledge bases across healthcare, finance, and scientific discovery. However, standard question-answering systems operate under the flawed assumption that all required facts are present in the knowledge base. In reality, operational databases and knowledge graphs are inherently incomplete, constantly evolving, and filled with missing connections. When faced with missing facts or multi-step questions, standard language models frequently hallucinate incorrect responses, while traditional graph-retrieval tools fail because the necessary factual paths do not exist.

This article evaluates a novel hybrid question-answering system called GLOW, which integrates graph neural networks with LLMs to answer questions accurately over incomplete knowledge graphs.

The primary objective is to demonstrate that combining structural graph predictions with natural language reasoning enables robust inferences even when critical direct links are absent.

items.title: Factory's @TaylorTheSavage warns that companies need to treat AI agents as potential bad actors, rat...
items.content:
Factory's @TaylorTheSavage warns that companies need to treat AI agents as potential bad actors, rather than blindly trusting black-box systems they can't control:

"For a consumer of models, you obviously don’t have control of the upstream model. So it does become a harness problem, and then it becomes an environment problem. Where are you letting the agents actually run, and what are you giving it access to?"

"This is what Satya was saying in his post too. It becomes the responsibility of the consumer of these models to treat them as potential bad actors. Very powerful risk factors within your organization, and build the controls around them to keep them in their box."

"A lot of other companies treat their harness just like a pure black box. ‘Here it is. Trust it. It’s really smart. You can’t see what it’s doing, but we promise it’s really smart.’ We have the opposite approach."

"Enterprise customers, big companies, they don’t like having black boxes sitting in their office that they don’t know what it does. Nobody does."
@FactoryAI

items.title: AIUC CEO @RuneKvist explains why you can't insure against human extinction, but insurance against sm...
items.content:
AIUC CEO @RuneKvist explains why you can't insure against human extinction, but insurance against smaller AI failures could still help prevent a $100B catastrophe:

"Take the example of extinction. You cannot underwrite that. It doesn’t really make sense."

"Imagine a loss of control scenario like Hugging Face. You can imagine a future Hugging Face that leads to hundreds of billions of dollars of damages. The guardrails you’d want insurers to audit overlap a lot with the guardrails you’d want for a $100 million loss or even a $10 million loss."

"An insurance layer that audits all the guardrails that would have prevented a $100 million loss will provide some of the guarantees you’d want against a $100 billion loss, even though we don’t have insurance for that."
@aiunderwriting

items.title: AIUC CEO @RuneKvist warns that rogue AI agents have become a serious threat in just 6 months, and th...
items.content:
AIUC CEO @RuneKvist warns that rogue AI agents have become a serious threat in just 6 months, and the incidents we've seen so far may only be warning shots:

"We’ve proven that insurance and standards can work at the agent level, at the application level, and we’re now bringing that to the foundation model layer, where we think the most meaningful societal risks are."

"Rogue agents were not a risk six months ago, and clearly we’ve found an astounding number of small incidents over the last six months. Those are not the last ones to be found."

"This is a problem that no one has a solution for, and the potential for damages is astoundingly large. In some ways, we’ve been extremely lucky with the warning shots we’ve had so far. Hugging Face is not that much damage."

"If you extrapolate that forward three, four, five, six months, that is the thing I would pay most attention to if I was running a frontier lab."
@aiunderwriting

I've been using Kylon for a few days already, and I really like it.

This is a "company harness".

It takes your people + your data + your agents and puts them into the same workspace. Basically, everyone can work and collaborate in the same space.

I'm using it with my local Codex. You can also connect it to Claude Code, Devin, or use a Kylon Cloud account. When you run it locally, Kylon hands off any agentic task to my Codex. It works pretty well!

If I had to guess, most companies will move eventually to a model like this. It just makes sense.

items.title: AIUC CEO @RuneKvist predicts that as AI agents get smarter, they'll make fewer mistakes, but their f...
items.content:
AIUC CEO @RuneKvist predicts that as AI agents get smarter, they'll make fewer mistakes, but their failures could become far more catastrophic:

"I basically predict that every generation will have fewer of the incidents than we saw with the previous model. The frequency will go down, but a new level of severity gets unlocked."

"If you read the report on Hugging Face, there’s a number of basic mistakes that the agents make that means they don’t get as far as they could have."

"Think of the Enron scandal. It takes an enormous amount of intelligence to cook the books for that long in that sophisticated a manner. It’s required that you can succeed at smaller tests to pull something like that off. I suspect that’s also how the curve might look for loss of control."
@aiunderwriting

items.title: .@AdamThierer calls out the AI safety community's obsession with p(doom), arguing that putting a per...
items.content:
.@AdamThierer calls out the AI safety community's obsession with p(doom), arguing that putting a percentage on human extinction doesn't make it science:

"Everybody wants to know what’s your p(doom)? I’m never one to play that game because we’re talking about subjective probabilities or feelings dressed up as hard math. Just because there’s a percentage after these guesses does not mean that they’re hard science."

"We should absolutely think about those risks, but we shouldn’t sell it to the public and policymakers like we have exactly a 10% chance of all dying within the next five to 10 years. That’s silliness."

"That’s fueling the panic that we see around AI and robotics and advanced computation right now. That’s speculative catastrophism masquerading as science, and that’s bad for us."
@RSI

"Everybody wants to know what’s your p(doom)? I’m never one to play that game because we’re talking about subjective probabilities or feelings dressed up as hard math. Just because there’s a percentage after these guesses does not mean that they’re hard science."

"We should absolutely think about those risks, but we shouldn’t sell it to the public and policymakers like we have exactly a 10% chance of all dying within the next five to 10 years. That’s silliness."

"That’s fueling the panic that we see around AI and robotics and advanced computation right now. That’s speculative catastrophism masquerading as science, and that’s bad for us."

@RSI

items.title: Getting an agent to work once is easy. Keeping thousands of them running in the cloud, every day, is...
items.content:
Getting an agent to work once is easy. Keeping thousands of them running in the cloud, every day, is where most teams get stuck.

@unreallabsai spent a year building exactly that, and just wrote down everything they learned.

The one I keep thinking about: their agents never hold your passwords. Every request leaves the sandbox through a proxy that adds the credentials on the way out, so an agent can't leak a key it never had.

Their open source harness also matches Codex on SWE-Marathon at 48% lower cost.

How many agents running right now are sitting on someone's API keys?

items.title: Introducing the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, benchmarking decision models across classificati...
items.content:
Introducing the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, benchmarking decision models across classification, tool calling, knowledge and reasoning. Jev leads among decision models; language models such as Claude Haiku 5.5 still deliver higher accuracy, but at much higher cost and latency

Decision models deliver structured answers or classifications with associated probabilities, offering faster responses and lower costs than using language models. The Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0 compares the capability, cost, and speed of decision models and also compares to language models.

Benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0:

➤ AA-Omniscience-Decision: A private dataset of 500 questions adapted from the proprietary AA-Omniscience benchmark, measuring decision models’ knowledge and tendency to hallucinate

➤ HLE-MultiChoice: 513 text-only multiple-choice questions from Humanity’s Last Exam, testing decision models’ reasoning capabilities

➤ When2Call: A tool-calling benchmark from NVIDIA, testing whether models can correctly decide to call a tool, request clarification, decline to answer, or respond directly, evaluating capabilities relevant to agentic workflows and tool routing

➤ WildGuardTest: A safety benchmark evaluating models’ classification capabilities across harmful user requests, assistant refusals, and harmful responses. We use a subset of 835 of the original 1,725 test rows where all three human annotators agreed on all three labels, after excluding questions that consistently trigger model refusals

Key results:

➤ Jev 1.13 leads the Decision Index, and sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier: Jev 1.13 from @typesafeai scores 58 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ahead of GLiDE (54) from @fastinoAI and Microsoft-Decision-1 (54) from @Microsoft. Decider v1.1 27B from @perplexity_ai has the lowest Cost per 1M Tasks at $17, with Microsoft-Decision-1 ($31) and Jev 1.13 ($42) also on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. Celeris-1 Decision has the fastest Time per Task at 0.06 seconds, more than 2x faster than Jev 1.13 (0.13 seconds per task)

➤ Decision models are poorly calibrated on knowledge and reasoning tasks: Across almost all probability levels for chosen answers, accuracy falls below that probability for all decision models. This gap is largest on AA-Omniscience-Decision and HLE-MultiChoice, while most models are relatively well-calibrated on WildGuardTest (classification) and When2Call (tool calling)

➤ Decision models offer significant speed and cost advantages over language models, but trail on knowledge and reasoning: On classification and tool-calling tasks, leading decision models perform comparably to language models while being significantly faster and cheaper. However, language models substantially outperform on knowledge and reasoning. Claude Haiku 5.5 (Low) scores 61 on the Decision Index, 3 points ahead of Jev 1.13, but takes 1.4 seconds per task vs. 0.13 seconds (11x slower) and costs $184 per 1M Tasks vs. $42 for Jev 1.13 (4.4x more expensive)

We will continue to develop the Artificial Analysis Decision Index to help developers and companies better understand when and how to use decision models.

items.title: If an agent saves an engineer 2 hours to implement a feature but collectively costs the team 3 hours...
items.content:
If an agent saves an engineer 2 hours to implement a feature but collectively costs the team 3 hours in alignment and review, the ROI is negative.

Isolated chats are suboptimal in team environments because they lack the context of what the team already discussed and decided. The Kylon app fixes this by running Claude Code and Codex in a shared, multiplayer environment. Agents gain real-time visibility into team consensus and architecture decisions.

items.title:
Post-training of LLMs typically relies on supervised finetuning or reinforcement learning.

While su...
items.content:
Post-training of LLMs typically relies on supervised finetuning or reinforcement learning.

While supervised finetuning is computationally efficient, it frequently exhibits poor generalization and can degrade pre-existing model capabilities, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting.

Conversely, reinforcement learning achieves superior generalization by training on data generated by the model itself, but it requires massive compute budgets, depends on reliable reward signals that are scarce in complex tasks, and suffers from low sample efficiency. 

This article addresses this operational dilemma by introducing a framework that enables on-policy supervised fine-tuning, aiming to deliver the generalization benefits of reinforcement learning alongside the computational efficiency of standard supervised pipelines.

The primary objective of the article is to establish a theoretical method for quantifying when training data aligns with a model’s native distribution, and to demonstrate that aligning data and training objectives with this internal distribution surpasses offline reinforcement learning methods while cutting computational costs.

.@AdamThierer argues that effective altruism (EA) risks becoming a quasi-religion that treats morality like a math problem and society like something to be optimized:

"Effective altruism is rooted in utilitarianism, and there’s a lot we can learn from utilitarianism. But the problem is when one seeks to convert utilitarianism into a sort of quasi-religion and treat morality like a math problem to be solved through various types of interventions and elitist planning."

"Too many people in the EA community suffer from a sort of fatal conceit of thinking that really complex moral, social, and technological problems can be solved through rational optimization and enlightened central planning."

"We’ve seen this script before. Morality’s not a math problem, and society and economies can’t be easily optimized."
@RSI

items.content:
This is like sending your agent to college.

This is an open-source engine that you plug into your agents and improves them without retraining. This gives them access to a huge indexed content library + search capabilities:

• Source code
• Engineering guidelines
• Documentation
• Security information

Let's say you want to check your application for vulnerabilities:

1. You choose a security collection that's relevant to the task
2. It downloads its sources and builds a local index
3. The agent searches for relevant information
4. It then uses that evidence when reviewing your code

And it's all free!

items.title: Samsara's @brendanodris explains why the AI revolution looks different outside the San Francisco bub...
items.content:
Samsara's @brendanodris explains why the AI revolution looks different outside the San Francisco bubble, where it's about helping truck drivers get home safely, not booking concert tickets:

"The vehicle is a means to an end. Whether it’s an agent, whether it’s an assistant, whatever the form, that’s just a means to an end."

"For me, it’s about a driver who’s pulled over on the side of a road and they need to know where they should pull in because they’re approaching their limit."

"Whether that’s a voice agent or not, who cares? They have an issue. They need a solution. ‘I’ve got 10 minutes of driving time left. Where do I pull in that’s safe?’ It’s dark. It’s late."

"This isn’t AI for AI’s sake, like book me a concert ticket. This is really, how do I get home at nighttime? Make sure that I’m wearing my seatbelt, no harsh braking, that I’m not using my phone."

"There’s a certain extra privilege that we get that we’re actually getting more people home at nighttime. And that’s a fun thing to work on."
@Samsara

items.content:
Pronunciation Robustness measures whether Text to Speech models correctly pronounce challenging text across four categories, with human reviewers judging each clip against pre-agreed accepted pronunciations. Drama 3 Preview leads overall at 93.2%.

➤ Standalone Terms: Drama 3 Preview ranks #1 at 95.9%, ahead of Eleven v3 Conversational at 95.1% and Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at 93.7%.

➤ Preserving Exact Sequences: Drama 3 Preview ranks #1 at 86.3%, ahead of SpaceXAI TTS at 85.7% and HeyGen Voice at 83.4%.

➤ Expanding Shorthand: Drama 3 Preview ranks #2 at 93.6%, behind Eleven v4 at 94.1% and ahead of Eleven v4 Turbo at 91.9%.

➤ Contextually Appropriate: Drama 3 Preview scores 95.3%, with Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS leading at 97.9%.

items.title: Training modern foundation models requires massive computational budgets, with standard workflows pr...
items.content:
Training modern foundation models requires massive computational budgets, with standard workflows predominantly relying on hand-designed optimization algorithms such as Adam.

While machine learning researchers have long pursued learned optimizers—algorithms whose update mechanisms are themselves trained on data to discover faster, superior training paths—practical adoption has stalled. Prior learned optimizers suffered from poor generalization to new domains, instability when scaling to large neural networks, and astronomical training costs; for instance, the previous state-of-the-art optimizer, VeLO, consumed approximately 4,000 TPU months of computation yet failed to reliably train models exceeding 600 million parameters.

This article demonstrates that an effective, general-purpose learned optimizer does not require enormous training compute. The primary objective is to present and evaluate Celo2, an optimizer architecture and training framework designed for optimization stability, out-of-distribution generalization, and high compute efficiency.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/n5Upgg408X

items.title: As organizations deploy large reasoning models to tackle complex tasks such as competitive mathemati...
items.content:
As organizations deploy large reasoning models to tackle complex tasks such as competitive mathematics and software coding, generating a single response is often insufficient for reliable results.

To scale accuracy, system designers typically choose between two inference strategies: generating multiple candidate solutions independently and pooling them (parallel sampling) or prompting the model to iteratively refine its previous answers in a conversational chain (sequential sampling).

While sequential self-refinement is intuitively appealing and theoretically more expressive, practical deployments consistently show that parallel sampling achieves superior accuracy. Understanding why sequential refinement lags behind is critical for technical leaders who must optimize compute expenditure, operational latency, and task accuracy.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/H8Jt3cOCdX

items.summary: Burkov discusses a paper comparing parallel sampling versus sequential self-refinement for scaling reasoning-model accuracy, noting that despite sequential refinement's theoretical appeal, parallel sampling consistently wins in practical deployments on accuracy, latency, and compute.

items.title: Today we are rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally in the Gemini API, to Pro + Ultra in Gemini App, an...
items.content:
Today we are rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally in the Gemini API, to Pro + Ultra in Gemini App, and Ultra subs in Antigravity!

Argon is a huge step forward for Gemini, and a labor of love. This model has been battle tested by over 100,000 people at Google over the last month, with so much new innovation, ambition, and hard work baked into this release. The team has been heads down over the last 6 months working to make this possible across the stack (research, infra, safety, eng, etc).

We rolled the model out to cyber defenders as part of our fairwind program and early access customers over the last 2 weeks, it has been amazing to see and talk to folks who are now using this model daily. Seeing the models writing capability, raw knowledge and persistence for coding, paired with new features like 1M token output when the model needs to work more has gotten me even more excited about our path ahead.

This is just the start of the Gemini 4 era. As you saw with 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash, our iteration speed with Gemini is fast : ) Now with Gemini 4 Argon to work from, I am cannot wait to see the progress continue, and most importantly see what this new model enables for the world. 

This is such a special moment in the arc of technology, as millions of people everyday tackle problems they could never have thought possible before. Gemini 4 Argon was built to help you tackle the hardest problems. I have personally felt this spark with Argon and hope you do too. Onwards!!

items.title: Google DeepMind's @tulseedoshi reveals the new safety system built into Gemini 4 Argon that monitors...
items.content:
Google DeepMind's @tulseedoshi reveals the new safety system built into Gemini 4 Argon that monitors the model's reasoning and intervenes when it starts going off the rails:

"There has been very few discussions about Argon where we have not been talking about safety and alignment. It’s been a core aspect of every single part of our decision-making."

"We’ve been putting in guardrails at all aspects of the model, whether that’s at the input level, within the model itself, or monitoring the model."

"When you think about something like misalignment, what we’re launching Argon with is basically a monitor for the chain of thought."

"We want to be monitoring the model’s thoughts, identifying if the model is gonna veer off the rails, and then actually being able to intervene. That is a protection that makes us feel more confident in rolling out the model today."
@GoogleDeepMind

items.title: Robotics currently faces a major bottleneck in scaling manipulation capabilities because collecting ...
items.content:
Robotics currently faces a major bottleneck in scaling manipulation capabilities because collecting direct robot demonstrations through human teleoperation is labor-intensive, expensive, and limited to specific hardware setups.

While ordinary videos of humans performing everyday tasks represent a vastly more scalable alternative, using them directly is notoriously difficult due to embodiment mismatch—a human body moves very differently than a mechanical arm or humanoid—and the fact that motions viable in one scene often fail on a robot due to joint limits, reachability boundaries, or physical collisions.

This article addresses this challenge by evaluating whether a system can learn reusable object manipulation skills entirely from human video demonstrations and adapt them to varied robots and environments without requiring any real-world robot demonstrations in target tasks.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/w7PpLkRCDN

items.title: Deploying safe LLMs remains a critical challenge because conventional safety mechanisms rely heavily...
items.content:
Deploying safe LLMs remains a critical challenge because conventional safety mechanisms rely heavily on extensive databases of harmful prompts paired with scripted refusals. While this established approach attempts to teach models to reject specific dangerous requests, attackers regularly bypass such guardrails using rephrased prompts, novel jailbreaks, or previously unseen attack vectors. Compounding this vulnerability, existing defense techniques often require compiling hundreds of thousands of toxic examples and can severely degrade the model's normal operational capabilities on standard, everyday tasks.

This article demonstrates a novel defense framework called Latent Personality Alignment (LPA). The main objective is to evaluate whether training language models to embody abstract, positive personality traits—without exposing them to any harmful examples during training—can reliably produce strong adversarial defenses while preserving general utility.

As a result, this defense method trains language models on fewer than 100 abstract personality traits to match the safety of models trained on over 150,000 harmful examples while reducing error rates against unseen attacks by 2.6 times.

items.title: Busy morning back from vacation. I've been resharing a ton of news this morning, especially from Goo...
items.content:
Busy morning back from vacation. I've been resharing a ton of news this morning, especially from Google who just launched a new model, and Apple who just announced a bunch of hardware, along with a bunch of startups in AI space (see my profile).

I was just talking with execs at @hm (big fashion brand) about the future of fashion. 

How will brain computer interfaces, glasses, robots, autonomous cars, change our fashion? 

For one, if you had a humanoid in your business, you will want a uniform for your robot, and if you brought it home, you would want a variety of outfits to make it nicer to look at, at minimum. 

Just think of a world where there are millions of robots walking around our cities. Do we want them all to look the same? Heck no. And that's a place where America will have a lot to say, even if China is way ahead in robotics. (And they have a lot of stores in China too).

Hey @radbackwards thinking of you, since you are ahead of most in building a fashionable home robot. I think there will be a sizeable market someday for dressing up your Neo. I don't want mine to be dressed the same as the one that @wholemars has.

But I was also thinking of @reservoirfarms. How textiles are grown in America was something they were interested in. And farmers aren't seen as fashionable, but I disagree, even when out in the field they have a unique fashion sense that's utilitarian, from boots and hats, but they like to party on the weekends and dress up just like every one else.

But brands like them can help introduce new ideas to lots of people, and brain computer interfaces are clearly coming, and are opening up new fashion needs. 

Interesting way to end vacation, was my first meeting after getting back home for the first time in 10 days. 

Now back to catching up on all the AI news that's breaking from Google and others. 

What would you want to show a fashion brand about the future? Are you building a company that has a potential impact on fashion? @hthieblot got any startups we should get on the calendar to come see?

It's so nice to be back home.

items.title: @pmddomingos I haven't seen an approach yet that can learn an equivalent of Codex from data, but thi...
items.content:
@pmddomingos I haven't seen an approach yet that can learn an equivalent of Codex from data, but this recent paper you posted, where they used RL to finetune an LLM that rewrites an existing harness based on its performance on examples of some kind of task, seems like a promising direction. Unfortunately, the experiments in the paper are too simplistic to claim that one can start with an ordinary loop and arrive at something like Codex or Claude Code.

I was reluctant to write about the harness because scientifically it's not much, but with an LLM used to continuously patch harness code (and avoid overfitting), it becomes much more fun.

This is one of the most complex and coolest textbook releases I've made on @ChapterPal so far: Lessons in Electric Circuits by Tony R. Kuphaldt (2026).

It's not a single book. It's a series of six (6) volumes!

The six textbooks contain everything needed to learn electronics from scratch, from the foundations of electricity and electromagnetism to semiconductor theory, transistors, number systems, Boolean algebra, combinational logic, and microprocessors.

The six volumes are:

1. Direct Current (DC)

2. Alternating Current (AC)

3. Semiconductors

4. Digital Circuits

5. Electronics Engineering Reference

6. DIY Electronics Projects

The curriculum has 7,389 illustrations and 3,620 exercises organized into 188 worksheets.

Read the curriculum with an AI tutor: https://t.co/kRg3CTi3hy

All the exercises are adapted for the exercise-solution AI tutor, which doesn't provide solutions but looks at the student's progress and gives hints grounded in the learned content.

All textbooks on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account.

I've been working out since 2018 with traditional gym e...
items.content:
Today, I did my first workout using Tonal. 

I've been working out since 2018 with traditional gym equipment, and I honestly expected Tonal to be gimmicky.

It is not. I actually liked it a lot.

Here is the thing: although digital resistance feels weird compared to the real thing, Tonal's built-in intelligence makes up for it in spades:

• You get spotter mode, so you can push to failure when working alone, like I always do.

• You get burnout mode, so the machine adjusts the weight down when you are gassed, so you can keep repping out.

• You get smartflex mode, so the machine auto-adjusts the weight (up or down) based on how easy/hard it is for me.

There are a few more modes, but I haven't tested them yet.

Let's see how it feels over the next few weeks, but so far, I'm really happy with this thing.

I'm not sponsored by Tonal in any way. I bought mine after testing it at my friend's house. It's freacking expensive, but I'm sure I'll make good use of it.

@demishassabis My friend and Bell Labs colleague John S. Denker was the inspiration for the Mitch character in the movie. 
He got into Caltech at age 16, played a central role in a number of pranks (like winning a McDonald's sweepstake by printing thousands of entries using a high-speed printer), built the first handheld electronic game (a football game which he licensed to Mattel), then decided to do a PhD in physics at Cornell and joined Bell Labs upon graduation.

Same

> Switzerland is nice, but not great. Worked with a couple of villages there, huge potencial and surprisingly affordable real estate vs cost of life in more rural areas. 

What do you think is not great?

> America is out for me, the quality of the food and environment is too low. 

It highly depends on which city/area you stay and how much you pay I think, the high end is super clean and healthy food (think Whole Foods)

> Being close to the ocean is important for me so probably Florianopolis, Porto, Sicilia and... Dubai? 

Yes I also love there, Floripa is great, we'll stay in Brazil too and have a house there
